title: HYDRAULIC AND GEOMETRIC CONTROLS ON INFILTRATION PERFORMANCE IN STORAGE–RECHARGE DRAINAGE SYSTEMS

HYDRAULIC AND GEOMETRIC CONTROLS ON INFILTRATION PERFORMANCE IN STORAGE–RECHARGE DRAINAGE SYSTEMS

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Ayudia Hardiyani Kiranaratri, M Bisri, Runi Asmaranto, Dian Sisinggih, Very Dermawan

ABSTRACT

Urbanization has reduced natural infiltration capacity, increased surface runoff, intensified flood risks, and limited groundwater recharge. Storage–recharge drainage systems incorporating infiltration boxes have been proposed as a sustainable drainage alternative; however, the relative influence of hydraulic and geometric parameters on infiltration performance remains insufficiently quantified. This study investigated the effects of soil hydraulic conductivity, inflow discharge, and infiltration box geometry on infiltration discharge in a storage–recharge drainage system.Two soil permeability group, three inflow discharges, three infiltration box area, three infiltration box depth, three box spacing and three channel bed slope experimental scenarios were tested in a laboratory-based physical model (486 total experimental scenarios). A new method was developed based on a water-balance approach to compute infiltration discharge. To quantify the relationships between the variables of interest and infiltration discharge, Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses were performed along with simple linear regression. Soil hydraulic conductivity was identified as the primary control factor exhibiting the best correlation with infiltration discharge (r=0.684) and explaining 46.7% of variability observed (R² = 0.467). The second most influential variable was inflow discharge (r = 0.563; R² = 0.317). The infiltration discharge was only weakly influenced by the area, depth and slope of the infiltration box and channel spacing. However, increasing the size of infiltration boxes improved low-permeability performance. These results show that the infiltration performance in storage–recharge drainage systems is determined mainly by hydraulic conductivity and inflow conditions, while the efficacy of geometric changes has site-specific soil moisture characteristics. The findings provide an empirical foundation for optimizing infiltration-based drainage systems to maintain urban flood control and groundwater recharge.
